subject: The largest scoring component was stuck at maximum-bearish for 79% of every historical scan ever run
body:
Version: SLS(181) with 68 timeframe reads corrected. Sending after a completed version, as asked.

THE BIG ONE, AND IT INVALIDATES A LOT OF WHAT I TOLD YOU EARLIER TODAY.

Every multi-timeframe read in the EA passed the CHART bar index straight into a higher-timeframe
moving-average call. The chart is M5. The export scans back 50,000 bars. Asking for the 40,000th D1
bar requests something that does not exist. MT4 returns 0, both averages come back 0, the comparison
is false, and the timeframe silently reports BEARISH.

Measured: comp_mtf, the largest component at plus or minus 36 against everything else at 29 or less,
sat at exactly -36.00, its maximum bearish value, for 79.3% of the 50,000-bar export. The score was
short on 88.7% of bars over a period when the market rose 2.4%. That is not a bearish model. It is a
stuck one.

Fixed in two passes: 18 reads in the three scoring functions, then 50 more in the eleven calibration
functions, including regime IC measurement and the weight search itself. 68 total. Run 5, running
now, is the first calibration in this project history on a scorer that was not partly a constant.

WHAT THAT MEANS FOR EVERY NO-EDGE RESULT THIS PROJECT HAS PRODUCED. They were all measured through
this. The pessimism was never earned. We genuinely do not know yet.

Concretely the headline sign flipped: bar-level expectancy is +0.0017R on the clean export, not the
-0.0140R I reported earlier. Still indistinguishable from zero, so not measurably losing rather than
winning, but the direction of every previous claim was wrong.

WHAT I RETRACTED TODAY, four times.

1. The sign-flip finding, IC -0.33, which I called the first result ever to clear the bar. It was
   look-ahead, my own bug: the feature compared each bar to the NEXT one. Causally it is -0.013
   against a non-flip -0.010. Nothing. A research agent spotted it from the shape of the claim
   before seeing any of my code.
2. The conviction gradient. Measured on the pinned component. On clean data a proper trend test
   gives p = 0.33.
3. The barrier shortfall. Two valid methods disagree, and I had argued for the one I preferred.
4. The trend-exhaustion strength. I quoted z = -3.2 from a Fisher transform; with real regression
   standard errors on ranks it is t = -1.4 to -2.0.

The pattern: every claim I made from a Fisher-transformed IC came back weaker under a proper
standard error. That is now a standing rule rather than a lesson.

WHAT SURVIVES, and it is architectural rather than statistical.

The system has three directional inputs, not six. signalDir is computed from MTF plus momentum, and
volatility, volume and session are each MULTIPLIED by it. They cannot vote on direction, only
amplify a decision already made. Pattern can overturn it on 3.1% of bars. Direction equals sign(MTF)
alone on 85.5% of bars.

And sign(comp_mtf) predicts the forward move on 49.6 to 50.4% of bars at every horizon. A coin flip.

So the per-regime weight search optimises six weights, three of which cannot change which way a
trade goes, only how hard it is taken. Nine regimes never validating is not a data problem. It is a
search over the wrong parameters.

ONE PRACTICAL LEAD, offered as a suppression rather than a strategy. Hour 23, the rollover window,
runs -0.2665R in the first half of the sample and -0.2481R in the second, win rate 0.286 against
0.40 elsewhere. The hour pattern as a whole is noise: 14 of 24 hours agree in sign across halves,
p = 0.27. But 23 is consistent in both halves AND has a mechanism, since spreads widen most exactly
there and the export excludes spread entirely. Suppressing it moves mean R from +0.0017 to +0.0129.
Still inside noise at n_eff 2500, so it should be pre-registered, not switched on.

37 of 45 criteria. C1.3, C2.2, C6.1 and C6.2 earned today.
